# Psychiatric drug poisoning

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Toxicologic disorders > Psychiatric drug poisoning*

[Original Article Link](/library/qF0CQ3)

---

## Summary

<u>Poisoning</u> from the ingestion of psychiatric drugs (e.g., <u>antidepressants</u>, <u>antipsychotics</u>, or <u>mood stabilizers</u>) may occur as a result of an accidental or intentional overdose, changes in metabolism or excretion, or interactions with other drugs or food. Clinical features vary depending on the medication, amount ingested, and duration of therapy. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with supportive studies including toxicological studies (e.g., serum drug levels) for certain substances, <u>ECG</u>, and <u>laboratory studies</u>. Management is primarily supportive with early involvement of the local Poison Control Center. Symptomatic patients generally require admission for further monitoring and treatment.




See also “<u>Sedative-hypnotic drug overdose</u>” and for prescription stimulants, see “<u>Stimulant intoxication and withdrawal</u>.”

---

## Antidepressant overdose

### Overview [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)




* <u>Antidepressants</u> increase the availability of <u>neurotransmitters</u> (e.g., <u>serotonin</u>, <u>norepinephrine</u>).

* Features of <u>antidepressant overdose</u> depend on the mode of action, e.g.:

* <u>Tricyclic antidepressants</u> (<u>TCAs</u>) can cause <u>anticholinergic syndrome</u>.

* <u>SSRIs</u> and <u>SNRIs</u> can cause <u>serotonin syndrome</u>.

* <u>Bupropion</u> and <u>SNRIs</u> can cause <u>features of stimulant intoxication</u>.

* <u>MAOIs</u> can cause <u>hyperadrenergic symptoms</u> and <u>serotonin syndrome</u>.

* Overdoses of certain substances (particularly <u>TCAs</u>, <u>venlafaxine</u>, and <u>citalopram</u>) are associated with significant cardiotoxicity. [[3]](/library/LoWwcm0)

* <u>Morbidity</u> from <u>antidepressant overdose</u> varies by drug class; it is greatest for <u>TCAs</u> and <u>MAOIs</u>. [[4]](/library/noW7cm0)





### Approach to antidepressant overdose [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### Diagnostics




* <u>Antidepressant overdose</u> is predominantly a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on <u>toxicological history and physical examination</u>.

* Perform a <u>toxicological risk assessment</u> and obtain routine diagnostic studies. 

* Common <u>ECG</u> findings include <u>QTc</u> and QRS prolongation.

* <u>Urine drug screens</u> can help diagnose <u>TCA poisoning</u> and determine coingestants, but the results may be unreliable.

* Serum drug levels are often unobtainable or not available in time to inform acute management.

* Serial <u>ECGs</u> and/or <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u> are commonly indicated.





#### Initial management




* Perform an <u>ABCDE approach in poisoning</u> and initiate resuscitation.

* Call the local Poison Control Center: In the US, the Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222.

* <u>Manage agitation</u> and <u>toxic seizures</u> with <u>benzodiazepines</u>.

* Provide <u>supportive care for poisoned patients</u>, e.g., <u>fluid resuscitation</u>, <u>treatment of hypoglycemia</u>, and <u>electrolyte repletion</u>.





#### <u>GI decontamination</u>




* <u>Activated charcoal</u> is recommended for the majority of recent ingestions in patients who are alert and/or have a protected <u>airway</u>.

* <u>Gastric lavage</u> may be appropriate for recent <u>TCA</u> or <u>MAOI poisoning</u> because of the associated increased <u>morbidity</u>.





#### Substance-specific management




* Consider <u>sodium bicarbonate</u> for <u>TCA</u>, <u>SNRI</u>, and <u>bupropion overdose</u> with QRS prolongation or <u>ventricular arrhythmias</u>.  [[6]](/library/DgW1xk0)

* Initiate symptom-specific management, e.g., <u>manage serotonin syndrome</u>.

* For life-threatening symptoms, consider <u>lipid emulsion therapy</u> and/or <u>ECMO</u> under specialist guidance. [[7]](/library/HnXKuA)

* See sections on “<u>TCA overdose</u>,” “<u>SSRI overdose</u>,” “<u>SNRI overdose</u>,” “<u>MAOI poisoning</u>,” and “<u>Bupropion overdose</u>” for additional recommendations.





#### Consults and disposition [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Guidance for disposition is limited. Disposition should be determined based on individual risk in consultation with Poison Control.




* Consult <u>psychiatry</u> for all intentional overdoses.

* Admit symptomatic patients for continuous monitoring.

* Admit to the <u>ICU</u> if hemodynamic stabilization, <u>mechanical ventilation</u>, or dialysis is required.

* Consider discharge after ≥ 6 hours of observation for asymptomatic patients with a normal <u>ECG</u>.

## Tricyclic antidepressant overdose

### Mechanism of action [[8]](/library/1KW22m0)




* Cardiac fast <u>sodium</u> channel inhibition

* <u>Muscarinic ACh receptor</u> inhibition

* A<sub>1</sub>-<u>adrenergic receptor</u> inhibition

* <u>H<sub>1</sub> receptor</u> inhibition

* GABA<sub>A</sub> inhibition





### Clinical features [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[8]](/library/1KW22m0)[[9]](/library/WKWP2m0)




* <u>Anticholinergic syndrome</u>;  (e.g., <u>hyperthermia</u>; , <u>delirium</u>, <u>ileus</u>, <u>urinary retention</u>)

* Cardiotoxicity: <u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Neurotoxicity</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u> (e.g., <u>lethargy</u>, <u>coma</u>)

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Respiratory <u>depression</u>

* <u>Myoclonus</u>

* <u>Extrapyramidal syndrome</u>





### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




<u>Tricyclic antidepressant</u> (<u>TCA</u>) overdose is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>, but studies may be performed to support the diagnosis and determine severity.




* ECG findings of TCA poisoning ;  [[8]](/library/1KW22m0)

* <u>Sinus tachycardia</u>

* Prolonged QRS interval   [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* <u>Prolonged QTc interval</u>

* Terminal R wave in aVR

* Ventricular and <u>supraventricular arrhythmias</u>

* Toxicological studies

* Serum <u>TCA</u> levels:

* Correlate poorly with <u>poisoning</u> severity  [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* > 1 mcg/mL are generally associated with severe symptoms (e.g., <u>seizures</u>, <u>dysrhythmias</u>)

* <u>Urine drug screens</u>:

* Commonly test for the presence of <u>TCAs</u>

* May be falsely positive in patients who take medications such as <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>cyclobenzaprine</u>, <u>antipsychotics</u>, or <u>antimuscarinics</u> [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: to assess <u>electrolyte</u> levels

* <u>VBG</u>: to assess for <u>acidemia</u>





> [!TIP]
> Serial <u>ECGs</u> should be performed to detect dynamic changes. [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)




> [!NOTE]
> The three Cs of tricyclic <u>poisoning</u>: Convulsions, Coma, and Cardiac conduction abnormalities (<u>prolonged QTc interval</u>).




![ECG abnormalities in tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) toxicity](media/ik2cy7xkntq4wlnxtkrntrua.jpg)

ECG abnormalities in tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) toxicity




### Management [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### Initial management




* Follow the <u>approach to antidepressant overdose</u>.

* Provide <u>supportive care</u>.

* <u>Secure the airway</u> in patients with <u>altered mental status</u> or <u>hemodynamic instability</u>.

* Provide <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u>.

* Initiate <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>.

* Consider <u>GI decontamination</u>.

* <u>Activated charcoal</u>: for ingestions within the past 2 hours in alert or intubated patients

* <u>Gastric lavage</u>: may be considered for ingestions within the past 2 hours in intubated patients





#### Symptom-specific management




* QRS interval > 100 ms and/or ventricular <u>dysrhythmias</u>

* Administer hypertonic <u>sodium bicarbonate</u> (<u>off-label</u>). DOSAGE  [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[6]](/library/DgW1xk0)[[7]](/library/HnXKuA)

* Consider a subsequent <u>isotonic bicarbonate</u> infusion to maintain <u>pH</u> between 7.50 and 7.55.

* Obtain serial <u>ECGs</u> to monitor response to treatment.

* <u>Toxic seizures</u>

* First-line treatment: <u>benzodiazepines</u>

* Second-line treatment: <u>barbiturates</u>

* Refractory <u>seizures</u>: <u>general anesthesia</u>

* <u>Phenytoin</u> is contraindicated because it worsens cardiovascular toxicity and is not effective.

* See “<u>Phase-based acute seizure management</u>” for dosages.

* Life-threatening cardiotoxicity: Consider <u>lipid emulsion therapy</u> and/or <u>ECMO</u>. [[7]](/library/HnXKuA)





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>TCA overdose</u>, <u>sodium bicarbonate</u> can help overcome <u>sodium</u> channel blockade and prevent ventricular <u>dysrhythmias</u>, reduce conduction delays, and increase blood pressure. [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Class IA antiarrhythmics</u>, <u>class IC antiarrhythmics</u>, and <u>class III antiarrhythmics</u> are contraindicated in <u>TCA overdose</u>. [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Physostigmine</u> is contraindicated in patients with suspected <u>TCA overdose</u> because it can precipitate <u>cardiac arrest</u>. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### Disposition [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Admit patients requiring mechanical ventilatory support and/or with <u>hemodynamic instability</u> to the <u>ICU</u>.

* Admit patients with clinical features of cardiotoxicity or <u>neurotoxicity</u> for <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>.

* Consider discharging asymptomatic, nontachycardic patients with a normal <u>ECG</u> after ≥ 6 hours of observation.

## Lithium poisoning

### Definitions [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Acute <u>lithium poisoning</u>: toxic effects caused by acute <u>lithium</u> ingestion in patients not therapeutically taking <u>lithium</u>

* Acute-on-chronic <u>lithium poisoning</u>: toxic effects caused by acute <u>lithium</u> ingestion in patients therapeutically taking <u>lithium</u> who have achieved steady-state concentration

* Chronic <u>lithium poisoning</u>: toxic effects caused by a gradual increase in serum <u>lithium</u> levels in patients therapeutically taking <u>lithium</u>





### Etiology [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Excessive intake

* Increase in prescribed dose (<u>lithium</u> has a narrow therapeutic window)

* Accidental or intentional overdose

* Decreased excretion

* <u>Renal insufficiency</u>

* <u>Hypovolemia</u> (e.g., due to <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, or water restriction)

* Medications that increase the renal absorption of <u>lithium</u>

* <u>Thiazide diuretics</u>

* <u>NSAIDs</u> (except <u>aspirin</u>)

* <u>ACE inhibitors</u>

* <u>Angiotensin receptor blockers</u>

* Other medications: <u>tetracyclines</u>, cyclosporines, <u>metronidazole</u>





### Clinical features [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[18]](/library/HmYKSp)




* Symptoms by type of <u>poisoning</u>

* Acute <u>lithium poisoning</u>

* Early: gastrointestinal symptoms

* Hours after ingestion: neurological symptoms

* Acute-on-chronic <u>lithium poisoning</u>: Gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms may occur simultaneously.

* Chronic <u>lithium poisoning</u>: Neurological symptoms predominate.

* Gastrointestinal: <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, and <u>diarrhea</u>

* Neurological

* <u>Altered mental status</u>, confusion

* <u>Somnolence</u>, <u>coma</u>

* <u>Delirium</u>, <u>encephalopathy</u>, psychomotor impairment

* Coarse <u>tremors</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>fasciculations</u>, <u>myoclonus</u>

* <u>Ataxia</u>, slurred speech, <u>nystagmus</u>

* <u>Hyperreflexia</u>

* <u>Extrapyramidal syndrome</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Lithium</u> slowly redistributes from the serum into the <u>CNS</u>. Therefore, in acute <u>poisoning</u>, GI symptoms predominate early, while in chronic <u>poisoning</u>, neurological symptoms predominate. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




<u>Lithium poisoning</u> is diagnosed based on history, clinical features, and serum <u>lithium</u> levels.




* Serum <u>lithium</u> level

* Toxic effects occur when serum <u>lithium</u> levels are > 1.5 mEq/L.  [[19]](/library/ZKWZUm0)

* Collect samples in <u>lithium</u>-free tubes.

* <u>BMP</u>: to evaluate for <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>hypernatremia</u>, <u>hypercalcemia</u>) and markers of renal dysfunction (e.g., elevated <u>creatinine</u>)

* <u>ECG</u> findings

* <u>T-wave flattening</u> or <u>inversion</u>

* <u>Prolonged QTc interval</u>





### Management [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### Initial management




* Perform an <u>ABCDE approach in poisoning</u> and initiate resuscitation.

* Call the local Poison Control Center: In the US, the Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222.

* Provide <u>supportive care for poisoned patients</u>, e.g., ventilatory support, <u>fluid resuscitation</u>, and <u>electrolyte repletion</u>.

* Discontinue <u>lithium</u> therapy.





#### <u>GI decontamination</u>




* <u>Whole bowel irrigation</u> may be used in patients with severe symptoms due to sustained-release preparations. [[20]](/library/nFX7i-)

* <u>Activated charcoal</u> does not bind to <u>lithium</u>.

* <u>Ion exchange resins</u> (e.g., <u>sodium polystyrene sulfonate</u>) are not routinely recommended.





#### <u>Indications for hemodialysis</u> [[21]](/library/Qwaui5)




* <u>Hemodialysis</u> is recommended in patients with either of the following:

* Serum <u>lithium</u> concentration > 4 mEq/L and <u>kidney</u> dysfunction

* <u>Altered mental status</u>, <u>seizures</u>, or life-threatening <u>dysrhythmias</u>

* <u>Hemodialysis</u> may be considered in patients with any of the following:

* Serum <u>lithium</u> concentration > 5 mEq/L

* Confusion

* Serum <u>lithium</u> concentration not expected to decrease to < 1 mEq/L within 36 hours





#### Monitoring and disposition




* Obtain serial serum <u>lithium</u> levels every 2–4 hours until two consecutive declining levels are observed.  [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Symptomatic patients should be admitted for further monitoring and treatment.

* Admit patients with <u>indications for hemodialysis</u> to the <u>ICU</u>.

* Consider discharging asymptomatic patients with <u>lithium</u> levels within the therapeutic range after 6 hours (immediate-release) or 12 hours (sustained-release).





> [!WARNING]
> Clinical features rather than absolute serum <u>lithium</u> levels should guide treatment. [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Diuretics</u>, osmotic agents, and <u>carbonic anhydrase inhibitors</u> are contraindicated in <u>lithium poisoning</u>, as they can worsen <u>hypovolemia</u> and increase <u>lithium</u> retention. [[2]](/library/Y11n2f0)
